items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. On August 6, a question in a school quiz in Kerala’s Kasaragod district sparked a major political row and led to the suspension of the teacher who set the quiz. Which freedom fighter received the "most severe punishment" from the British, the quiz master Guru Prasad asked, to which the students were expected to answer, VD Savarkar. Guru Prasad, a teacher at AUP School Pallathadukka in Kumbla, has been suspended pending inquiry by the Kerala Education Department. The Director of General Education (DGE) has also directed the Deputy Director of Education, Kasaragod, to initiate departmental disciplinary proceedings against the teacher and conduct a detailed inquiry into the matter. Reports suggest that Guru Prasad plans to approach the Kerala High Court over the state government's action. items.title: Plea in Supreme Court alleges Odisha trying to bypass law on DGP appointment
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to urgently hear a public interest litigation (PIL) petition alleging that the Odisha government was attempting to circumvent the top court's judgment on the appointment of the State's Director General of Police (DGP) by including ineligible officers in the selection panel. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana agreed to list the matter on Wednesday. Senior Advocate P Chidambaram , appearing for the petitioner, mentioned the matter. He alleged that the State withdrew a panel of officers sent to the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and was now preparing a fresh list. He further contended that the State was attempting to promote an Additional Director General of Police (ADGP) to the rank of DGP and then include the officer in the fresh panel sent to the UPSC. Taking note of the submissions, CJI Kant said, “They (UPSC) are well aware of who is eligible and who can be considered. If a panel of ineligible officers is being sent, we expect the UPSC to act in accordance with our directions." items.title: Gen Z lawyers more open to mediation: Supreme Court Justice Kotiswar Singh
items.summary: Gen Z lawyers are more open to mediation than older generations and are likely to take it seriously if given proper training and are shown that it can offer a viable career, Supreme Court Justice N Kotiswar Singh recently opined. The judge recalled asking around 15 interns how mediation was taught in their law colleges. Their responses indicated that it was treated “just like another, just a by-the-way kind of subject”. He contrasted this with the importance given to moot court competitions and called for a similar push for mediation in colleges and universities. Greater exposure would allow students with different aptitudes to consider mediation as a career rather than merely treating it as a compulsory subject, he said. “ I don't want to criticise my generation, but this Gen Z generation are very, very sensitive. Given the proper training, the proper approach, they are going to accept....If we are able to show the positive aspects of this profession, that you can have a really good future profession in this mediation, they are going to take it very seriously ,” he said.
